note.explanation: Newton’s laws describe everyday motion very accurately, but they are not exact for every situation. For very small particles or objects moving close to the speed of light, relativistic mechanics is needed.
examples: A car moving at an ordinary road speed is well described by Newton’s laws.
An elementary particle moving close to the speed of light needs relativistic mechanics.
note.checkAnswer: Newton’s laws are a good approximation for everyday motion, but are not exact for very small objects or objects moving close to the speed of light.
note.simple: Newton’s laws work very well for ordinary things we see and use. For tiny particles or extremely fast objects, Einstein’s relativistic mechanics is more suitable.
note.title: Limitations of Newton’s Laws
steps: Use Newton’s laws for objects and speeds we meet in everyday life.
Recognise that they are not exact for all types of motion.
For elementary particles moving close to the speed of light, use relativistic mechanics.
note.answer: Relativistic mechanics is applicable to elementary particles having velocities close to the speed of light.

written.text: Why has not Newton's first law been proved on the Earth?
written.finalAnswer: It is not possible to test Newton’s first law perfectly on Earth because friction and other forces act on objects; a completely force-free situation cannot be produced.

rubric.why: The answer must identify forces that affect motion on Earth.
rubric.description: Identifies friction and other forces acting on objects on Earth.
rubric.how: State that friction and other forces cannot be completely eliminated.

rubric.why: This links the forces present on Earth to the difficulty of testing the law perfectly.
rubric.description: Explains that a completely force-free situation cannot be produced, so the law cannot be proved perfectly.
rubric.how: Conclude that the ideal condition required to test the law is unavailable on Earth.

modelAnswer: On the Earth, friction and other forces act on objects and cannot be completely eliminated.
Therefore, a completely force-free situation cannot be produced to prove Newton’s first law perfectly.

examTips: This section is most likely to be tested as a short-answer or conceptual question about when Newton’s laws are not exact.
For full marks, state both the limitation (very small objects or velocities close to the speed of light) and the suitable theory (relativistic mechanics).
If asked for the general conclusion, mention that Newton’s laws remain a good approximation for everyday motion.

example.question: When are Newton’s laws not exact, and what mechanics is applicable in that case?
example.answer: Newton’s laws are not exact for elementary particles having velocities close to that of light; relativistic mechanics is applicable.

explain.title: Newton’s laws work very well in everyday life
explain.body: The objects and speeds we come across in ordinary life are described with very high accuracy by Newton’s laws.

explain.title: There are limits to their accuracy
explain.body: Newton’s laws are not exact for every kind of motion. The section points to objects that are very small or moving close to the speed of light.

explain.title: Relativistic mechanics is used for extreme cases
explain.body: For elementary particles moving at velocities close to the speed of light, relativistic mechanics developed by Albert Einstein is applicable.

explain.title: Remember the key conclusion
explain.body: Newton’s laws provide a good approximation unless an object is small enough or moving close to the speed of light.

mistakes: Do not write that Newton’s laws are useless or always wrong; they work with very high accuracy for everyday motion.
Do not confuse “close to the speed of light” with “at rest” or ordinary speeds.
When asked what applies to elementary particles moving close to light speed, name relativistic mechanics.
Do not omit the small-object limitation when asked to state the section’s overall conclusion.
